A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, retaining the KL-PCB and KL-PCDB algorithms despite substantial expansion and retitling. All 23 pages of v1 and 38 pages of v2, including mathematical displays, tables, algorithms, references, and appendices, support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports algorithms, sample-complexity theorems, and proofs in Sections 2–3 and Appendices A–B. Table 1 summarizes theoretical bounds; no original empirical outcomes are reported.

after.justification: v2 remains theoretical throughout Sections 2–4 and Appendices A–F. Its constructed bandit instances support mathematical lower bounds, rather than reported experiments or simulations.

M1.justification: v2 retains the pessimistic KL-PCB and KL-PCDB procedures as Algorithms 1 and 3. It adds f-CB and f-CDB as Algorithms 2 and 4, using unadjusted least-squares or maximum-likelihood reward estimates followed by f-divergence policy optimization. Removing pessimistic bonus subtraction for these new procedures is a substantive algorithmic extension.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or tasks in reported training or evaluation. The new f-divergence settings and hard-instance constructions extend theoretical scope, without adding empirical coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version experimentally evaluates comparison methods. Xiong et al. (2024) and Zhao et al. (2024) remain analytical comparators in Table 1; additional literature comparisons concern theoretical positioning.

E3.justification: Neither version reports experimental splits, evaluation metrics, training budgets, or testing procedures. The i.i.d. reward and Bradley–Terry feedback models are theoretical assumptions, and the new lower-bound constructions are not experimental protocols.

E4.justification: Neither version contains original ablations, robustness experiments, sensitivity tests, error analyses, or empirical case studies. The added hard instances and derivations support theoretical proofs.

E5.justification: Neither reports repeated runs, seeds, empirical uncertainty estimates, or significance tests. High-probability guarantees and concentration lemmas are mathematical results rather than experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Neither version reports measured performance or qualitative empirical findings. The changes to analytical sample-complexity results, including those summarized in Table 1, are assessed under T1.

T1.justification: v1 adapts earlier lower bounds under constant coverage; v2 adds explicit coverage-dependent lower-bound constructions in Appendices B.4 and E.2. Assumption 3.1, Theorems 3.2–3.4, and the dueling extensions introduce strongly convex f-divergence guarantees with order η/(αε) sample complexity, up to entropy and logarithmic factors, supported by convex-conjugate and Hessian arguments. Equation 2.2 also restores the reference-policy factor omitted in v1.

C1.justification: The central contribution expands from nearly optimal KL-regularized learning under single-policy concentrability to distinguishing coverage requirements across regularizers. v2 claims necessary multiplicative coverage dependence for KL and coverage-independent fast rates for strongly convex f-divergences, including dueling feedback. Its conclusion also qualifies v1's suggestion of a complete KL characterization by acknowledging a remaining gap.

C2.justification: v2 explains why stronger regularization can keep learned and optimal policies sufficiently close to the reference policy to avoid coverage dependence. Remarks 2.8–2.11 distinguish density-ratio and function-class concentrability and limit the matching-bound interpretation to a special case. Section 5 explicitly acknowledges the remaining KL gap and restricts the broader results to twice continuously differentiable, strongly convex f.

D1.justification: Neither provides software, numerical solver settings, hardware, runtime, or code/data access information. The retained KL estimators and analytic bonus specifications are unchanged; the new abstract algorithms do not add corresponding implementation disclosures.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens positioning around regularizer-dependent coverage. Appendix A distinguishes its offline setting from Foster et al. (2025)'s hybrid setting and Zhao et al. (2025)'s online setting. New references support f-divergence motivation and convex-analysis proofs, including Gabbianelli et al. (2024), Penot (1994), and Zhou (2018), while some peripheral citations are removed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. The earlier comparison discussion moves to Appendix A, while much of v1's main-text dueling algorithm and proof material moves to Appendices D–E. The narrative is reorganized around two regularizer classes, with accompanying notation and terminology changes.

P2.justification: Table 1 is substantially rebuilt: v1's contextual/dueling-bandit columns and coverage indicator become regularizer-specific upper/lower-bound rows and comparison-method columns with explicit parameter dependencies. The table moves earlier, two new algorithm displays are added, and the retained KL-PCDB display moves into Appendix D.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's proposed f-divergence extension, adds coverage-dependent lower-bound constructions, and states limitations more clearly. However, new Algorithms 2 and 4 maximize reward plus divergence, contradicting the subtraction in Equation 3.1 and their proofs. Theorem D.3 and Remark D.4 also use D² concentrability where Appendix E.2 bounds density-ratio concentrability C. These unresolved inconsistencies affect central new algorithms and guarantees, preventing a reliable judgment of net overall improvement.
